title: Enaughquamuck — Former Inlet Area
summary: Enaughquamuck marked a limit in seventeenth-century agreements over coastal resources within Unkechaug territory. Its exact inlet is uncertain; this pin provides orientation to the barrier beach south of Mastic.
address_label: Present-day Smith Point, NY — coastal orientation point, not the exact former inlet
map_geometry_source: Broad coastal context: Strong 2011 p.51 and Strong 2018 p.39; exact former inlet unknown. Point is NPS Wilderness Visitor Center coordinate 40.732430,-72.866970 for modern public orientation only.
why_this_matters: The coastline moved, but the records still preserve Native authority, named leaders and negotiated resource rights. An approximate map location can introduce that history without pretending the seventeenth-century shoreline is known exactly.
introduction_title: A Coastal Name and Unkechaug Resource Rights
introduction_content: Enaughquamuck appears as a boundary in agreements concerning the beach and drift whales—whales washed ashore—within Unkechaug territory. The history includes the Unkechaug sachems Tobacus and Winecroscum, Wyandanch, Lyon Gardiner and Anthony Waters. Strong places these negotiations within a landscape of Native authority over coastal resources.2, 3
history_content:
Tooker dates the agreement to July 28, 1659. It concerned whale bodies and bones coming ashore along the coast from Kitchaminchoke to Enaughquamuck. The agreement reserved fins and tails to the Indigenous parties rather than conveying every part of the whales.1, 3

Strong’s account explains that Tobacus and Winecroscum were included because the shore lay within their territory. These transactions concern particular resource rights; they should not be read as proof that Indigenous connections with the coast ended.3
translation_content: Tooker interpreted the name as referring to the far extent of a fishing place. This is his historical linguistic interpretation. His 1901 discussion also acknowledges that he could not identify the former inlet’s exact position.1
whereintheworld_title: Location and Why the Pin Is Approximate
whereintheworld_content:
The evidence supports a broad barrier-beach setting south of Mastic, not a precise inlet coordinate. Strong’s 2011 history places the probable old inlet south of the Carmans River; his 2018 discussion suggests somewhere south of the Mastic Peninsula near Pattersquash Island. These descriptions narrow the coastal region but do not identify the same exact point.2, 3

The pin is deliberately placed at the modern Wilderness Visitor Center beside Smith Point County Park as a public orientation point for that coastal landscape. The National Park Service supplies this modern location. It is not claimed as the historical inlet, a whaling station or a place where the agreement was signed.4, 5

Tooker warned that the beach contained traces of several former openings. No historical inlet polygon is drawn, and the name is not equated with today’s Moriches Inlet or the breach opened by Hurricane Sandy in 2012. Follow posted National Park Service and county access rules when visiting the modern shore.1, 4
